transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Two Senate races and numerous House races have yet to be called from the elections.
But as NPR's Tamara Keith reports, Democrats are on pace for their largest Senate majority
in more than a decade.
The swing in the House is even more dramatic.
To give a sense of scope, here are just two of the more improbable Democratic wins.
Nevada's second congressional district has been represented by a Republican since it
was created in the early 1980s.
That race was called overnight for Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson.
And Congressman Shamari figures from Alabama was targeted by redistricting, drawn out of
his hometown.
In 2024, that district as drawn now would have gone to Trump by 14 points.
Figures won by more than seven points.
There hasn't been this kind of a swing in the House toward Democrats since the post-Nixon
Watergate backlash.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
Midterm voters weighed in on ballot measures across the country on topics ranging from
abortion to taxes to guns.
NPR's Rachel Treisman has more.
Voters in 39 states, D.C. and the Northern Mariana Islands considered a total of 146
statewide ballot initiatives this midterm season.
Several states moved to protect LGBTQ rights, including Virginia, which removed its constitutional
ban on same-sex marriage.
Others, like Colorado and Arizona, restricted transgender students' access to school sports.
Taxes were on the ballot, too.
Residents voted to cut property taxes for homeowners.
Tennessee voters prohibited their government from collecting a statewide property tax.
Three states voted to protect access to abortion.
Massachusetts voted in support of gun control legislation, while Idaho residents voted to
choose an official state gun.
Rachel Treisman, NPR News.
President Trump says he believes costs from the war in Iran played a role in his party's
defeat in the elections.
And P.S. Hadil Al-Shelchi reports Iran may have been trying to achieve that by closing
the Strait of Hormuz.
After the U.S. and Israel started the war with Iran in February, Iran blocked the Strait
of Hormuz for eight months.
Retail gasoline prices have surged by nearly 44 percent since the war.
Trita Parsi is an Iran expert with the Quincy Institute.
He says there was one big reason that drove voters to elect the Democrats.
Absolute fury with the cost of living situation, which in and of itself was a result of an
Iranian strategy to create an energy crisis for the precise reason of defeating Trump
and the Republican Party.
But Parsi says Iran also knows that those who want to go to war see the time before
the next Congress is sworn in as the last chance for an escalation.
Hadil Al-Shelchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Forecasters say there's flash flooding early this morning in parts of southeastern Tennessee
and northern Georgia.
The National Weather Service says this flooding is catastrophic and widespread.
Warnings are up for Polk County, Tennessee and Georgia's Fannin County.
There are evacuations underway.
The U.N. has released a new report finding a "staggering shortfall of funding to adapt
to the climate crisis," and Piers Julia Simon has more.
At the U.N. Climate Conference in Scotland in 2021, world leaders from wealthy countries
committed to increase funding for developing nations most vulnerable to severe storms,
floods, droughts, wildfires and sea level rise.
Yet, a new U.N. report says wealthy countries are falling short.
Many countries will need $305 billion a year by 2035 to adapt to climate change.
That's nearly 10 times more than what they're getting now.
Next week, countries gather in Turkey for this year's U.N. Climate Conference, where
they will discuss climate finance.
The U.S. federal government will not be in attendance, but some Democratic lawmakers
will.
Julia Simon, NPR News.
Authorities in Europe say airline flights are disrupted today because of several bomb
threats made against passenger planes.
No devices have been found, and no injuries are reported.
The Vatican says that Pope Leo will leave tomorrow for a long-planned trip to South America.
He is being cared for by doctors after the Pontus lung surgery, rather lung cancer surgery,
last month.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Democrats on pace for largest Senate majority in over a decade; House swing dramatic, including Nevada's 2nd district flip
Voters decide statewide ballot measures on LGBTQ rights, property taxes, abortion, and gun policy across 39 states
Trump says Iran war costs contributed to GOP election defeat; Iran reportedly blocked Strait of Hormuz to pressure voters
Flash flooding catastrophic in southeastern Tennessee and northern Georgia; evacuations underway in Polk and Fannin counties
UN report finds wealthy countries far short of climate adaptation funding, needing $305 billion annually by 2035
Bomb threats against passenger planes disrupt European airline flights; no devices found, no injuries reported
Pope Leo to leave for South America trip while recovering from lung cancer surgery last month
